source_text: Ἐδύνατο μέντοι παραδεξάμενος ἢ συγχωρήσας ὁ Κέλσος τὸ προεγνωκέναι αὐτὸν τὰ συμβησόμενα αὐτῷ ἐξευτελίζειν μὲν τοῦτο δοκεῖν, ὅπερ πεποίηκεν ἐπὶ τῶν δυνάμεων, γοητείᾳ φάσκων αὐτὰς γεγονέναι, καὶ ἐδύνατό γε λέγειν ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀπὸ μαντειῶν, τῶν ἐν οἰωνοῖς ἢ ὄρνισιν ἢ θυτικῇ ἢ γενεθλιαλογίᾳ, ἔγνωσαν τὰ ἀπαντησόμενα αὐτοῖς. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὐκ ἠθέλησε συγχωρῆσαι ὡς μεῖζον, τὸ δὲ τὰς δυνάμεις πεποιηκέναι παραδεξάμενός πως δοκεῖ αὐτὸ προφάσει γοητείας διαβεβληκέναι. Φλέγων μέντοι ἐν τρισκαιδεκάτῳ ἢ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτῳ οἶμαι τῶν Χρονικῶν καὶ τὴν περί τινων μελλόντων πρόγνωσιν ἔδωκε τῷ Χριστῷ, συγχυθεὶς ἐν τοῖς περὶ Πέτρου ὡς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, καὶ ἐμαρτύρησεν ὅτι κατὰ τὰ εἰρημένα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τὰ λεγόμενα ἀπήντησε. πλὴν κἀκεῖνος καὶ διὰ τῶν κατὰ τὴν πρόγνωσιν ἄκων ὡσπερεὶ οὐ κενὸν θειοτέρας δυνάμεως ἀπεφήνατο εἶναι τὸν ἐν τοῖς πατράσι τῶν δογμάτων λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus could (δύναμαι, impf.), however, having accepted (παραδέχομαι) or conceded (συγχωρέω) that he had foreknown (προγιγνώσκω, pf.) the things that would befall him, belittle (ἐξευτελίζω) this as to seeming (δοκεῖν) — which very thing he has done with the mighty works (δυνάμεις), saying they happened by sorcery (γοητεία) — and he could indeed say that many, from divinations (μαντεῖαι), those in omens (οἰωνοί) or birds (ὄρνιθες) or sacrificial art (θυτική) or casting of nativities (γενεθλιαλογία), knew (ἔγνωσαν) the things that would meet (ἀπαντάω, fut. ptc.) them. But this he did not wish (ἐθέλω) to concede, as greater (μεῖζον); but, having somehow (πως) accepted that he did the mighty works, he seems to have slandered (διαβάλλω) it under pretext (πρόφασις) of sorcery. Phlegon, however, in the thirteenth or fourteenth, I think (οἶμαι), of the Chronicles (Χρονικά), also gave (δίδωμι) to Christ the foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) about certain future things, having been confused (συγχέω, aor. pass.) in the things about Peter as about Jesus, and testified (μαρτυρέω) that according to the things said by him the things spoken came to pass (ἀπαντάω). Except (πλήν) he too, also through the things concerning foreknowledge, unwilling (ἄκων) as it were (ὡσπερεί), declared (ἀποφαίνομαι) that the word/teaching (λόγος) in the fathers (πατέρες) of the doctrines (δόγματα) is not empty (κενός) of more divine power (θειοτέρα δύναμις).
pass_b_english: Celsus could, however, have accepted or conceded that Jesus foreknew what would happen to him, and then made it seem a trivial thing, as he did with the miracles when he said they were done by sorcery. He could indeed have said that many people, through divination by omens, by birds, by sacrifices or by horoscopes, have known what was going to befall them. But this he would not concede, as being the greater thing; whereas he has in a way accepted that Jesus worked the miracles, and seems to have discredited this under the pretext of sorcery.

Phlegon, however, in the thirteenth or fourteenth book, I think, of his Chronicles, even granted Christ foreknowledge of certain future events, although he confused what concerned Peter, taking it as said of Jesus; and he testified that the things foretold turned out as Jesus had said. Yet even he, through what he says about foreknowledge, declared, as if against his will, that the teaching found in the fathers of our doctrines was not without a more divine power.

choices.why: ὡς μεῖζον: 'as being too great a thing' -> 'as being the greater thing' (comparative, not excess)

choices.term: συγχυθεὶς ἐν τοῖς περὶ Πέτρου ὡς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ
choices.why: συγχυθεὶς ἐν τοῖς περὶ Πέτρου ὡς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ: 'confused what concerned Peter with what concerned Jesus' -> 'confused what concerned Peter, taking it as said of Jesus' (Phlegon applied Peter material to Jesus)
checked: Phlegon's book number kept with Origen's 'I think'; ἄκων ὡσπερεί 'as if against his will' kept; δοκεῖν/δοκεῖ handling in the first and third sentences accepted

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

notes: Translated from the Greek of the staged Koetschau row only; Crombie (ANF) and Chadwick were not used.
Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.
2.14 ἐξευτελίζειν μὲν τοῦτο δοκεῖν is compressed Greek; 'made it seem a trivial thing' was kept as a defensible reading (the translator's note gives the alternative)
2.14 'the fathers of our doctrines': 'our' is a light clarifying addition for τῶν δογμάτων; kept

translator_notes: ἐξευτελίζειν μὲν τοῦτο δοκεῖν is compressed: either ‘belittle this, so that it would seem trivial’ or ‘belittle this supposed [foreknowledge]’; rendered ‘made it seem a trivial thing’. οἰωνοί and ὄρνιθες both mean birds of omen; rendered ‘omens’ and ‘birds’ to keep both terms. δυνάμεις = ‘mighty works’, rendered ‘miracles’ as in the surrounding chapters. Phlegon of Tralles, Chronicles (Olympiads), books 13 or 14 by Origen’s own uncertain recollection (‘I think’). ‘The fathers of our doctrines’ (τοῖς πατράσι τῶν δογμάτων) means the founders of the Christian teaching, Jesus and the apostles; kept literal. No Scripture quoted.
